rationale: B wins because it keeps the same three viable lanes but trims more of the speculative varnish. Its "Databricks says revenue run rate passed $3B, growing 60%, with an IPO still undated" is a clean markets angle with proof questions that would survive the first callback; A's "Banks and hospitals want AI models they can audit" smuggles in an audit claim the update did not give it. A has good instincts, but it gets a little too pleased with its own accountability language.
gaps_in_A: "Banks and hospitals want AI models they can audit" overclaims the product benefit. The update gives open license and fine-tuning, not auditability.

"regulated enterprises cannot send proprietary data to third-party inference APIs" is plausible, but asserted as buyer reality when the update only says Databricks positions the model against closed APIs.

"unaudited, on its own benchmarks, before any public filing" mashes revenue skepticism and benchmark skepticism into one headline. Self-reported benchmarks are supplied; unaudited revenue and public-filing framing need separate proof.
"The prevailing assumption in coverage of AI platform competition" is a broad media-zeitgeist claim with no support in the update.
gaps_in_B: "The company paired it with a signaled but undated IPO" implies the IPO signal is part of today's disclosure. The update only says Databricks has signaled an eventual IPO with no date.
"buyers who cannot send data outside their own environment" is a reasonable regulated-enterprise hypothesis, but it is still a hypothesis until a buyer or compliance source says it.
"Why a company with $3B in revenue is giving its foundation model away" overstates open license as giving the model away. The license terms decide whether that headline lives or dies.
"If a fresh news peg would sharpen the set, run `newsjack-detector` first" is process clutter. The supplied launch and revenue disclosure are already the peg; don't go hunting for decorative urgency.
